lessons.title: Personal Hygiene for Caterers
lessons.body:
As a home-based caterer, your body is the most direct route for germs to enter food. Start with a daily routine: shower before cooking, wear clean clothes, and tie back long hair. Keep fingernails short and unpolishedâdirt hides under nails. Remove all jewellery (rings, bracelets, watches) because they trap bacteria. If you have a cut or sore on your hand, cover it with a waterproof plaster and wear a glove over it. Never cook if you have diarrhoea, vomiting, or feverâyou can pass germs to food even if you feel slightly better.

Handwashing is your number one defence. Wash hands for at least 20 seconds with soap and warm running water. Scrub palms, back of hands, between fingers, and under nails. Rinse and dry with a clean cloth or paper towel. Wash hands before starting cooking, after using the toilet, after handling raw meat or eggs, after touching your face or phone, after taking out rubbish, and after cleaning. Keep a bucket with a tap or a large jug of water and soap near your cooking area if you donât have a sink.

Wear an apron that you only use for cooking. Wash it regularly, especially after handling raw meat. Avoid touching your face, hair, or phone while cooking. If you must sneeze or cough, turn away and cover with your elbow, then wash hands. Donât taste food with your finger or a spoon you then reuseâuse a clean spoon each time. If youâre sick, ask a healthy helper to cook, or reschedule the event. Your reputation depends on safe food.

Also, keep your workspace clean: wipe surfaces before and after cooking. Donât let pets or children near the cooking area. In many African homes, cooking is communal, but for catering, limit the number of people handling food. Train any helper in these same rules. A simple sign at the handwashing station reminds everyone. Remember, customers trust you with their healthâpersonal hygiene is non-negotiable.

lessons.title: Safe Food Handling Temperatures
lessons.body:
Bacteria that cause food poisoning multiply fastest between 5Â°C and 60Â°Câthe danger zone. In hot African climates, food can spoil in under two hours if left out. Your goal: keep cold foods below 5Â°C and hot foods above 60Â°C. Without a thermometer, use these cues: reheated food should be steaming hot throughout, and cold food should feel ice-cold to the touch. But a cheap digital probe thermometer (available at most markets) is your best tool. Calibrate it in ice water (0Â°C) before use.

Cooking temperatures: poultry (chicken, turkey) must reach 74Â°C in the thickest part. Minced meat and sausages: 71Â°C. Whole cuts of beef, pork, lamb: 63Â°C and rest for 3 minutes. Fish: 63Â°C or until it flakes. Eggs: cook until yolk and white are firm. Leftovers: reheat to 74Â°C. When cooking for a crowd, use the thermometer to check several pieces, not just one. If you donât have a thermometer, cook poultry until juices run clear and meat is no longer pink.

Cooling and storing: After cooking, divide large pots into smaller containers to cool faster. Never leave food out for more than 2 hours (1 hour if room temperature is above 32Â°C). Refrigerate within 2 hours. Store leftovers in shallow containers, covered, and use within 3 days. Reheat only once. For events, keep hot food in insulated containers or on a warm burner (above 60Â°C). Cold foods like salads and desserts should be kept in a cooler with ice packs. If youâre transporting food, use a cooler box and pack ice around dishes.

Thawing: Never thaw meat on the counter. Thaw in the fridge (plan ahead), in cold water (change every 30 minutes), or in the microwave if cooking immediately. Marinate in the fridge, not on the counter. When grilling or frying, ensure the inside is cooked, not just charred outside. Use a clean plate for cooked meatânever the same plate that held raw meat. These temperature rules are simple but save lives.

lessons.title: Cross-Contamination Prevention
lessons.body:
Cross-contamination happens when harmful germs from raw food, dirty surfaces, or hands get into ready-to-eat food. In a home kitchen, the biggest culprits are raw meat, poultry, eggs, and unwashed produce. The solution: separate everything. Use separate chopping boardsâone for raw meat (red), one for vegetables and cooked food (green or white). If you only have one board, wash it with hot soapy water between uses. Never cut vegetables on a board that just held raw chicken without washing it first.

Keep raw meat and eggs away from other foods in the fridge. Store raw meat on the bottom shelf in a sealed container so juices donât drip onto food below. Donât store eggs in the doorâtemperature fluctuates. Use separate utensils for raw and cooked foods. Never taste with the same spoon youâre cooking with; use a clean spoon each time. When grilling, donât put cooked meat back on the plate that held raw meat. Wash plates and utensils with hot soapy water after contact with raw meat.

Clean as you go. Wipe spills immediately, especially raw meat juices. Use paper towels or a cloth that you wash after each use. Sanitize surfaces with a bleach solution: 1 teaspoon (5 ml) of household bleach per 1 litre of water. Spray or wipe, leave for 1 minute, then air dry or wipe with clean water. For dishes, wash in hot soapy water, rinse, then soak in the bleach solution for 1 minute, then air dry. Donât dry with a dirty towelâair drying is safest.

Also, be careful with reusable shopping bags. Wash them regularly, especially if they carried raw meat. In many African markets, meat is wrapped in plastic or paperâdouble-bag it. When you get home, immediately put meat in the fridge or cook it. If youâre catering an event, pack raw and cooked foods in separate coolers. Label containers. Train helpers to follow these rules. Cross-contamination is invisible, but the resultsâfood poisoningâare very visible. Stay vigilant.

lessons.title: Cleaning and Sanitizing Procedures
lessons.body:
Cleaning removes dirt and grease; sanitizing kills germs. You need both. Start by scraping food scraps into the bin. Then wash with hot water, soap, and a scrub brush. For dishes, use three basins if possible: one with hot soapy water for washing, one with clean hot water for rinsing, and one with a sanitizing solution (1 teaspoon bleach per 1 litre water) for soaking. If you only have one basin, wash, rinse, then sanitize in a separate bucket. Air dry on a clean rackâdo not towel dry, as towels can recontaminate.

Surfaces: After each use, wipe counters with hot soapy water, then sanitize with bleach solution. Let it sit for 1 minute before wiping with a clean cloth or letting it air dry. For wooden cutting boards, scrub with salt and lemon to remove odours, then wash and sanitize. Plastic boards can go in the dishwasher if you have one. Replace boards that have deep grooves where bacteria hide. Clean your fridge weekly: remove shelves, wash with hot soapy water, rinse, and sanitize. Donât forget door handles, taps, and light switchesâthese are high-touch areas.

Equipment: Clean your thermometer probe with alcohol wipes before and after each use. Clean your cooler boxes with soap and water, then sanitize, and leave open to dry. Wash dishcloths and towels frequentlyâsoak in bleach solution, then wash with hot water. Use separate cloths for dishes and surfaces. Sponges harbour bacteria; replace them weekly or boil them for 5 minutes. If you use a dish rack, clean it regularly.

Schedules: At the end of each cooking day, do a deep clean: sweep and mop floors, wipe all surfaces, empty bins, and sanitize. For events, clean as you go. Have a bin for waste near your station, and take it out frequently. In Africa, water may be scarce; use a spray bottle with bleach solution to sanitize without rinsing. Always wash hands after cleaning. A clean kitchen is a safe kitchenâmake it a habit, not a chore.

lessons.title: Allergen Management
lessons.body:
Food allergies can be life-threatening. As a caterer, you must know the common allergens and prevent them from contaminating other foods. The big eight: peanuts, tree nuts, milk, eggs, fish, shellfish, soy, and wheat. In Africa, also watch for sesame, mustard, and sulphites. Even a tiny amount can trigger a reaction. Symptoms include hives, swelling, difficulty breathing, and vomiting. If a guest has a severe reaction, call for medical help immediately.

When a client books you, ask about allergies. Keep a written record. If you cannot guarantee an allergen-free dish, be honestâdonât risk it. For each event, plan a separate area for preparing allergen-free food. Use clean utensils, boards, and pans that have been washed and sanitized. If youâre cooking multiple dishes, prepare the allergen-free one first, or use separate equipment. Never use the same oil that fried fish for chips if a guest is allergic to fish. Read labels on packaged foodsâmany sauces and spice mixes contain hidden allergens like wheat or soy.

Cross-contact is the biggest risk. For example, if you make a peanut sauce and then use the same spoon to stir a stew, you can transfer peanut protein. Always wash hands and change gloves after handling allergens. Use separate serving utensils for each dish. Label dishes clearly: âContains nutsâ or âGluten-free.â At a buffet, place allergen-free dishes separately and use a clean serving spoon for each. If a guest informs you of an allergy at the event, take it seriouslyâdonât just pick out the allergen; the whole dish may be contaminated.

Have an action plan: keep antihistamines on hand? No, thatâs for the guest. Your job is to prevent exposure. If a reaction occurs, call emergency services, and if the guest has an epinephrine auto-injector, help them use it. Document everything. Training your helpers on allergens is crucial. In many African cultures, food is shared, but for catering, you must respect individual needs. A reputation for safety will win you repeat business.

lessons.title: HACCP Basics for Home Kitchens
lessons.body:
HACCP stands for Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points. Itâs a system to prevent food safety problems before they happen. For a home caterer, you donât need a formal certification, but you can apply the same principles. Start by identifying hazards: biological (bacteria, viruses), chemical (cleaning agents), and physical (hair, glass, bones). For each step in your cooking process, ask: what could go wrong? Then set controls.

The seven principles: 1) Conduct a hazard analysis. List all steps from shopping to serving. 2) Determine critical control points (CCPs)âsteps where you can prevent or eliminate a hazard. For example, cooking is a CCP because proper temperature kills bacteria. 3) Set critical limits: e.g., cook chicken to 74Â°C. 4) Monitor: use a thermometer. 5) Take corrective action if limits are not met: e.g., continue cooking until 74Â°C. 6) Verify: check that your system worksâreview records. 7) Keep records: write down temperatures, cleaning schedules, and any problems.

In a home kitchen, focus on key CCPs: receiving (check that meat is cold and fresh), storing (fridge below 5Â°C), cooking (proper temperatures), cooling (within 2 hours), reheating (74Â°C), and holding (above 60Â°C or below 5Â°C). Also, personal hygiene and cleaning are CCPs. Create a simple log sheet: date, food item, temperature, action taken. Keep it for at least 3 months. If you donât have a thermometer, get oneâitâs your most important tool.

Start small: pick one dish you cook often and map out the steps. Identify where things could go wrong. For example, making chicken stew: buy chicken (check cold), store in fridge, wash hands, cut on separate board, cook to 74Â°C, cool quickly, refrigerate. At each step, note what you do to keep it safe. Over time, this becomes second nature. HACCP is not just for big factoriesâitâs for anyone who wants to serve safe food. Your customers will notice the difference.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Food Safety and Sanitation for Home-Based Caterers

In home-based catering across Africa, your kitchen is your factory floor, your reputation, and your legal exposure all at once. A single case of food poisoning traced to your jollof, chapati, or wedding buffet can end a business that took years to build. Unlike a licensed restaurant, you rarely have a compliance officer watching over your shoulder â which means your standards are entirely self-enforced. This practical reference consolidates the six lessons in this module into a working document you can print, laminate, and pin to your kitchen wall.

The approach here is deliberately business-first. Every practice below either (a) protects you from a costly incident, or (b) helps you win larger, better-paying contracts with hotels, NGOs, corporate clients, and event planners who increasingly ask for food safety documentation before signing.

1. The Temperature Danger Zone: Your Single Biggest Risk

Bacteria that cause foodborne illness multiply fastest between 5Â°C and 60Â°C. In most African home kitchens â particularly where power is intermittent or refrigeration is shared â food spends far too long in this zone. The table below summarises the critical temperatures you must know by heart.

Table 1: Critical Food Safety Temperatures for Home Caterers
Stage Temperature Why It Matters
Refrigerator storage â¤ 5Â°C (41Â°F) Slows bacterial growth; ideal for dairy, cooked meats, and leftovers.
Freezer storage â¤ â18Â°C (0Â°F) Stops bacterial growth entirely but does not kill bacteria.
Poultry (chicken, guinea fowl, turkey) 74Â°C (165Â°F) internal Kills Salmonella and Campylobacter.
Minced meat, sausages 71Â°C (160Â°F) internal Ground meat distributes surface bacteria throughout.
Whole cuts (beef, goat, lamb) 63Â°C (145Â°F) + 3 min rest Safe for whole muscle; rest time kills surface organisms.
Fish and seafood 63Â°C (145Â°F) internal Flesh should be opaque and flake easily.
Reheating leftovers 74Â°C (165Â°F) within 2 hours Must be piping hot throughout; never reheat twice.
Holding hot food for service â¥ 60Â°C (140Â°F) Keeps food out of the danger zone during buffets.

Source: U.S. Food and Drug Administration, Food Code 2022, Chapter 3 (Food), Tables 3-1 and 3-2; adapted for metric use. Also consistent with WHO Five Keys to Safer Food (2023).

Practical African context: if your event is outdoors and you have no chafing dishes, use insulated coolers (the same ones used for drinks) to hold hot food above 60Â°C, and pre-heat bricks or stones wrapped in clean cloth as heat sinks. For cold items like kachumbari or salads, use a cooler with ice packs and keep it closed between servings.

2. Cooling and Storage Timelines

The most common failure in home catering is not cooking â it is cooling and storage. Large pots of stew, rice, or ugali left on the stove overnight are a bacterial incubator. Use the two-stage cooling method.

Table 2: Safe Cooling and Storage Timelines
Step Time Limit Method
Stage 1: 60Â°C â 21Â°C Within 2 hours Divide into shallow containers (â¤ 5 cm deep); use ice bath or cold water bath.
Stage 2: 21Â°C â 5Â°C Within 4 more hours Refrigerate uncovered until cool, then cover.
Total cooling window â¤ 6 hours If not achieved, discard. Do not serve.
Refrigerated leftovers (cooked) 3â4 days maximum Label with date and dish name.
Frozen cooked food 2â3 months Use airtight containers; rotate stock (FIFO).
Room-temperature display (buffet) â¤ 2 hours Discard anything left beyond this at outdoor events.

Source: U.S. Department of Agriculture, Food Safety and Inspection Service, Refrigeration and Food Safety (2023); World Health Organization, Five Keys to Safer Food Manual (2006, reaffirmed 2023).

3. Personal Hygiene: The Invisible Ingredient

Your hands, hair, breath, and clothing are the most direct route for pathogens into food. For home caterers working without a commercial kitchen, personal hygiene is non-negotiable and must be visible to clients.

  • Handwashing: Wash with soap and running water for at least 20 seconds before starting, after handling raw meat or eggs, after using the toilet, after touching your phone or money, and after coughing or sneezing. Keep a dedicated handwash station (jerrycan with tap, soap, and paper towels) separate from the food prep area.
  • Gloves: Gloves are not a substitute for handwashing. Change them between raw and cooked foods, and never wear the same pair for more than 30 minutes.
  • Hair and nails: Tie back or cover hair. Keep nails short, unpainted, and clean. Nail polish flakes are a physical contaminant.
  • Illness: If you have diarrhoea, vomiting, jaundice, or an infected cut, do not cook for clients. Have a backup plan. This is a business decision, not just a health one.
  • Clothing: Wear a clean apron and, where possible, a head covering. Change aprons between raw and cooked food prep.

4. Cross-Contamination Prevention

Cross-contamination is the transfer of harmful bacteria from raw food (especially poultry, eggs, and meat) to ready-to-eat food. In small kitchens, this happens through shared chopping boards, knives, cloths, and hands.

  • Colour-code your boards: Red for raw meat, green for vegetables, blue for fish, yellow for cooked food. If you cannot afford a set, use one board and wash it with hot soapy water between every task.
  • Separate storage: Store raw meat on the bottom shelf of the fridge, covered, so juices cannot drip onto ready-to-eat food.
  • Cloths: Use disposable paper towels or change cloths frequently. A damp cloth left on the counter is a bacterial sponge.
  • Utensils: Never use the same spoon to taste and stir. Never reuse a marinade that has touched raw meat unless it is boiled first.
  • Market bags: Raw meat and vegetables bought at the market should be transported in separate bags. Reusable bags must be washed after every use.

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING â DO NOT IGNORE

Never taste food to check if it is still safe, and never serve food that has been left out overnight "because it smells fine." Bacillus cereus, Staphylococcus aureus, and Clostridium perfringens produce toxins that are odourless, tasteless, and heat-resistant. If food has been in the danger zone for more than 2 hours, discard it. The cost of one lost pot of stew is nothing compared to the cost of a client's hospital bill, a lost contract, or a damaged reputation in your community.

5. Cleaning and Sanitizing

Cleaning removes visible dirt; sanitizing reduces invisible pathogens. You need both. For home caterers, a two-step process is sufficient: wash with hot soapy water, then sanitize with a diluted bleach solution (1 teaspoon of 5% bleach per litre of water) or a food-safe commercial sanitizer. Let surfaces air-dry â do not towel-dry with a cloth.

Focus on high-touch surfaces: countertops, fridge handles, taps, light switches, and your phone. Clean as you go â do not leave a mountain of dirty pots until the end, because that is when cross-contamination happens.

6. Allergen Management

Common allergens in African catering include groundnuts (peanuts), tree nuts (cashews, almonds), fish, shellfish, eggs, milk, wheat, and soy. Groundnut is the most dangerous in many West and East African contexts because it is used in soups, stews, and snacks, and reactions can be severe.

  • Ask every client, in writing, about allergies before the event.
  • Keep a separate small pot and utensils for allergen-free dishes.
  • Label all dishes clearly at the buffet, especially sauces and garnishes.
  • Never assume "a little bit won't hurt" â for a severely allergic guest, trace amounts can be fatal.
  • Keep an antihistamine in your kit and know the nearest clinic.

7. HACCP Basics for the Home Kitchen

HACCP (Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points) sounds corporate, but the logic is simple: identify where things can go wrong, set a limit, monitor it, and act if it fails. For a home caterer, your critical control points are usually:

  1. Receiving: Check meat, fish, and dairy for temperature and smell at purchase.
  2. Cooking: Verify internal temperatures with a probe thermometer.
  3. Cooling: Follow the two-stage cooling rule.
  4. Holding: Keep hot food above 60Â°C and cold food below 5Â°C.
  5. Service: Limit buffet time to 2 hours; discard leftovers.

Write these five steps on a single page, note the date and time each time you check, and keep the log. When a corporate client or NGO asks for your food safety documentation, this log is your proof â and often your competitive advantage over other home caterers.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • â Wash hands for 20 seconds before, during, and after food handling.
  • â Use a probe thermometer to verify 74Â°C for poultry and 71Â°C for minced meat.
  • â Cool large pots in shallow containers: 60Â°C â 21Â°C in 2 hours, then 21Â°C â 5Â°C in 4 hours.
  • â Keep raw meat on the bottom fridge shelf, covered, away from ready-to-eat food.
  • â Use separate boards and knives for raw and cooked food; wash between tasks.
  • â Hold hot food at â¥ 60Â°C and cold food at â¤ 5Â°C; never leave food in the danger zone over 2 hours.
  • â Ask every client about allergies in writing; label all buffet dishes.
  • â Sanitize high-touch surfaces with diluted bleach (1 tsp per litre) and air-dry.
  • â Record cooking, cooling, and holding temperatures in your HACCP log.

Further Reading (Free Official Resources)

  • WHO â Five Keys to Safer Food Manual (World Health Organization, free PDF).
  • U.S. FDA â Food Code 2022 (free, comprehensive food safety reference).
  • USDA FSIS â Food Safety Basics (free guides on storage, cooling, and handling).
  • FAO â Food Safety and Quality (Food and Agriculture Organization, includes Africa-specific guidance).
  • CDC â Food Safety Prevention (free, plain-language guidance for small food businesses).

Business takeaway: Food safety is not paperwork â it is the foundation of every contract you will ever sign. A caterer who can show a client a clean kitchen, a temperature log, and a written allergen policy will win the wedding, the corporate lunch, and the NGO contract. The practices in this reference cost almost nothing to implement, but they protect everything you are building.

quiz.q: What is the minimum time you should wash your hands to remove germs effectively?
quiz.explanation: Washing hands for at least 20 seconds with soap and water is recommended to effectively remove germs.

quiz.q: Which of the following should you remove before cooking?
quiz.explanation: Jewellery can trap bacteria and should be removed before handling food.

quiz.q: If you have diarrhoea, what should you do?
options: A) Cook anyway but wear gloves
C) Not cook and ask a healthy person to cook
quiz.explanation: You can pass germs to food even if you feel better, so you should not cook when sick with diarrhoea.

quiz.q: What is the danger zone for bacterial growth?
quiz.explanation: Bacteria multiply fastest between 5Â°C and 60Â°C, known as the danger zone.

quiz.q: What internal temperature should chicken reach to be safe?
quiz.explanation: Poultry must be cooked to 74Â°C in the thickest part to kill harmful bacteria.

quiz.q: How long can cooked food be left out at room temperature if it is above 32Â°C?
quiz.explanation: When room temperature is above 32Â°C, food should not be left out for more than 1 hour.

quiz.q: Which of these is a safe way to thaw meat?
quiz.explanation: Thawing in the fridge is safe because it keeps the meat out of the danger zone.

quiz.q: What should you do with a plate that held raw chicken before using it for cooked chicken?
options: C) Wash with hot soapy water
quiz.explanation: The plate must be washed with hot soapy water to remove bacteria from raw chicken.

quiz.q: How should you store raw meat in the fridge?
options: B) On the bottom shelf in a sealed container
quiz.explanation: Raw meat should be on the bottom shelf in a sealed container to prevent juices from dripping onto other foods.

quiz.q: What is the correct bleach solution for sanitizing surfaces?
options: A) 1 teaspoon bleach per 1 litre water
B) 1 cup bleach per 1 litre water
C) 1 tablespoon bleach per 1 litre water
D) 1 teaspoon bleach per 10 litres water
quiz.explanation: A solution of 1 teaspoon (5 ml) household bleach per 1 litre of water is effective for sanitizing.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid drying dishes with a towel?
options: C) It uses too much water
quiz.explanation: Towels can harbour bacteria and recontaminate clean dishes; air drying is safer.

quiz.q: What is the first step in cleaning dishes?
options: C) Scrape food scraps into bin
quiz.explanation: Scraping food scraps into the bin removes loose debris before washing.

quiz.q: How often should you replace sponges?
quiz.explanation: Sponges harbour bacteria and should be replaced weekly or boiled to sanitize.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a common allergen?
quiz.explanation: Peanuts are one of the big eight common allergens.

quiz.q: What should you do if a guest informs you of an allergy at the event?
options: A) Pick out the allergen from the dish
C) Take it seriously and provide a safe alternative
D) Ignore it if they don't have a reaction
quiz.explanation: Even a tiny amount of allergen can cause a reaction, so you must take it seriously and provide safe food.

quiz.q: Why should you use separate serving utensils for each dish?
options: B) To prevent cross-contact of allergens
C) To make the table look nice
quiz.explanation: Separate utensils prevent allergens from one dish contaminating another.

quiz.q: What does HACCP stand for?
options: A) Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points
B) Health and Clean Cooking Practices
D) Home Allergy and Cooking Control Plan
quiz.explanation: HACCP stands for Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points, a food safety system.

quiz.q: Which of these is a critical control point (CCP) in a home kitchen?
options: B) Cooking food to proper temperature
quiz.explanation: Cooking is a CCP because proper temperature kills harmful bacteria.

quiz.q: What should you do if a critical limit is not met, such as chicken not reaching 74Â°C?
options: B) Continue cooking until it reaches 74Â°C
D) Put it in the fridge
quiz.explanation: Corrective action means continuing to cook until the safe temperature is reached.

quiz.q: How long should you keep HACCP records?
quiz.explanation: Keeping records for at least 3 months helps verify your food safety system.

quiz.q: What is the most important tool for checking food safety temperatures?
quiz.explanation: A digital probe thermometer is essential for accurately checking food temperatures.

quiz.q: Which of these is a physical hazard in food?
quiz.explanation: Hair is a physical hazard that can contaminate food.

quiz.q: What should you do before preparing allergen-free food?
options: B) Wash and sanitize all equipment
quiz.explanation: All equipment must be washed and sanitized to prevent cross-contact with allergens.

quiz.q: How can you sanitize a wooden cutting board?
options: B) Scrub with salt and lemon, then wash and sanitize
D) Wipe with a dry cloth
quiz.explanation: Scrubbing with salt and lemon helps remove odours and bacteria, followed by washing and sanitizing.

quiz.q: What is the correct temperature for reheating leftovers?
quiz.explanation: Leftovers should be reheated to 74Â°C to ensure any bacteria are killed.

quiz.q: Why should you not store eggs in the fridge door?
options: C) They take up too much space
quiz.explanation: The fridge door temperature fluctuates, which can compromise egg safety.

quiz.q: What should you do with a cut on your hand before cooking?
options: B) Cover with a waterproof plaster and wear a glove
D) Put a bandage and continue
quiz.explanation: A cut must be covered with a waterproof plaster and a glove to prevent contamination.

quiz.q: Which of these is a chemical hazard?
quiz.explanation: Cleaning agents are chemical hazards if they contaminate food.

quiz.q: How often should you clean your fridge?
quiz.explanation: Weekly cleaning of the fridge helps prevent bacterial growth and odours.

quiz.q: What should you do if you have a severe allergic reaction?
options: B) Use an epinephrine auto-injector if available and call for help
quiz.explanation: For a severe allergic reaction, epinephrine is the first-line treatment and emergency help should be called.
